Building a Better Fellowship

Program

Over the past eighteen months we have run four cohorts of the fel‐

lowship, each with roughly forty participants drawn from govern‐

ment, industry and academia. The program was designed to give

mid-career professionals a structured way into AI governance

work, and the results have been encouraging, if not uniformly so.

This report summarises what we learned, what we would do differ‐

ently, and where the fellowship should go next. It draws on partici‐

pant surveys, interviews with hiring organisations, and our own

records of placements and follow-on projects.

Key findings

Participants who completed a capstone project were twice as

likely to change roles within six months.

Weekly facilitated discussions mattered more than reading

volume; satisfaction fell sharply when groups exceeded eight

people.

Employers valued the fellowship's network effects over its

curriculum, which surprised us.

Recommendations

1. Make the capstone mandatory and give every participant a

mentor from a hiring organisation.

2. Cap discussion groups at seven, and pay facilitators so that

quality stays consistent across cohorts.

3. Publish a short, honest impact report after every cohort, in‐

cluding the figures that flatter us least.

Finally, the fellowship's influence on participants' professional

identity was its most significant and least anticipated effect. Many

told us that the official certificate was beside the point; what

changed was their confidence that this field had a place for them.

Page 1 of 2Our efficiency improved over time as well: the fourth cohort cost

thirty percent less per participant than the first, mainly because of

better-organised logistics and a flourishing alumni volunteer

network.
